**Gunmen Kill at Least 23 at Tunisia's Bardo Museum**

TUNIS, Tunisia — Gunmen stormed the Bardo National Museum in the Tunisian capital on Wednesday, killing at least 23 people in an assault on one of the country's most famous cultural sites and on the tourism trade that its economy relies on.

The majority of the victims were foreign tourists, a number of whom had disembarked that morning from cruise ships moored in Tunis. Security forces brought an end to a standoff inside the museum by shooting two of the attackers, and dozens of people received treatment for injuries. The Bardo, home to one of the finest collections of Roman mosaics anywhere, stands beside the national parliament.

The assault has rattled a country frequently called the lone success story of the Arab Spring. Following the 2011 revolution that toppled President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, Tunisia approved a new constitution and held free elections. At the same time, it has become one of the biggest suppliers of foreign fighters to extremist groups in Syria and Iraq, where an estimated 3,000 Tunisians are thought to have signed up.

To Mabrouka M'Barek, a onetime member of Tunisia's National Constituent Assembly, those two facts are tightly connected. She argues that Tunisia has not managed to "recruit" its own citizens into society, so that many young people, especially in the poorer interior regions, feel they hold no stake in the new democracy. When the state gives them no place, she says, extremist groups are happy to supply one.

Her argument moves the focus away from policing and toward joblessness, regional inequality and political exclusion, the very grievances that drove the 2011 uprising.

Tunisian leaders have promised a forceful response, and investigators are trying to determine who planned the attack. But while the country grieves, many Tunisians are asking whether their young democracy can reach the next generation before the recruiters get there.

The upside is that people who work from home save both time and money, since there is no commute. Home also has its share of distractions, such as the television, pets, and relatives, and these can make concentrating hard. And when the office is in the bedroom, some people struggle to switch off at the end of the day.

Reaching for the Stars Without Neglecting Home

Critics have an obvious point to make. Governments pour billions into rockets, probes, and telescopes each year, yet millions of people still have no clean water, medical care, or education, so it seems natural to say the money should be spent here on Earth. But setting space exploration against earthly problems as if they were competitors gets wrong how progress works in both.

The argument against space funding hits hard emotionally. The price of one Mars mission might pay for hospitals or vaccination drives, and with people suffering today, reaching for distant planets can look like an indulgence of rich countries.

Still, the budgets are smaller than most people imagine. NASA gets under half a percent of the U.S. federal budget, a sliver next to defense or health spending. Even more significant is that space research pays for itself in practical terms. Satellites follow hurricanes, watch over crops, and record climate change. Water purification, medical imaging, and solar power have all benefited from technology first created for spaceflight. Space programs also push students toward careers in science and engineering.

So governments ought to keep funding space exploration, but with care: they should favor missions with clear scientific or social payoff and share costs through international cooperation. In the end, looking up often helps us look after the ground we stand on.

text: On big e-commerce platforms, product feeds mix organic recommendations with sponsored listings, and ad placement has usually been tuned to bring in as much advertising revenue as possible right away. That short-term view misses an important side effect: when ads are badly placed or too numerous, users may engage less with organic content, which lowers the platform's long-term value. This paper casts the allocation of ads in product feeds as a sequential decision problem, with the goal of maximizing organic traffic subject to limits on ad exposure and revenue. We put forward a reinforcement learning framework in which an agent decides, for each request, how many ads to insert into the feed and where, taking into account the user's context and the list of candidate items. Because engagement signals are sparse and delayed, our reward blends immediate click feedback with a learned estimate of how deeply users will browse afterward, and a constrained policy optimization scheme is used to meet platform-wide advertising targets. Offline experiments on large-scale logged data, together with online A/B tests on a leading e-commerce platform, show that the method considerably raises organic clicks and session length while keeping advertising revenue steady, and it beats fixed-slot and greedy allocation baselines.

text: FeSe offers an ideal platform for pinning down the electronic origin of rotational symmetry breaking in iron-based superconductors, because its nematic phase appears at around 90 K without any long-range magnetic order alongside it. We used high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy on mechanically detwinned single crystals to follow how the electronic structure changes, resolved by momentum and orbital character, through the nematic transition. At low temperature, the d_xz/d_yz splitting at the Brillouin zone corner is about 50 meV, which sets the characteristic nematic energy scale; near the zone center the splitting is far smaller, so the order parameter depends strongly on momentum. One result is especially striking: in the nematic state we see just one electron pocket, and within our experimental resolution the pocket expected at the Y point is missing. We examine the roles that orbital-selective correlations and the d_xy orbital play in suppressing it, and we argue that the anisotropic Fermi surface that results offers a natural explanation both for the strongly anisotropic superconducting gap and for the lack of magnetic order in FeSe.

text: The azimuthal angular decorrelation of dijet systems is a sensitive probe of QCD radiation patterns and of parton dynamics at small Bjorken x. We present here a study of jet azimuthal decorrelation in deep inelastic electron–proton scattering at the proposed electron–proton mode of the Future Circular Collider (FCC-ep), where a 60 GeV electron beam collides with a 50 TeV proton beam at a centre-of-mass energy of roughly 3.5 TeV. Events are simulated using leading-order and next-to-leading-order matrix elements matched to parton showers, and jets are reconstructed with the anti-kT algorithm inside a realistic detector acceptance. We measure the distribution of the azimuthal angle difference between the two leading jets as a function of jet transverse momentum, photon virtuality, and rapidity separation. A clear decorrelation appears and grows with rapidity separation, and we compare its size to predictions from DGLAP and BFKL evolution. The results show that FCC-ep will widen the accessible kinematic range by over an order of magnitude compared with HERA, allowing stringent tests of small-x QCD dynamics and possible sensitivity to gluon saturation effects.

# Richard III Laid to Rest Again in Leicester as Cumberbatch Delivers Tribute

King Richard III was finally reburied on Thursday at Leicester Cathedral, five hundred years after he died at the Battle of Bosworth, in a ceremony that combined medieval pageantry with modern celebrity.

Richard, the last Plantagenet king, was killed in 1485 and buried in a hurry in the church of the Greyfriars friary in Leicester. In the following centuries the site was built over and its location was lost. Then in 2012 archaeologists made a stunning discovery, finding his remains under a city council car park, and DNA tests against descendants of his sister later confirmed the identification.

On Thursday, 530 years after the king's death, his oak coffin was lowered into a grave inside the cathedral. Actor Benedict Cumberbatch, a distant cousin of Richard, was one of the participants, reading a poem that Poet Laureate Carol Ann Duffy had written for the occasion.

Historian Philippa Langley, whose campaign set the search for the grave in motion, said the find had led researchers to reconsider the king. Richard's reputation has long been molded mostly by Tudor chroniclers and by Shakespeare, who depicted him as a hunchbacked tyrant who killed his young nephews, the "Princes in the Tower," in order to take the throne.

Examination of the skeleton revealed that Richard suffered from severe scoliosis but did not have a withered arm, and that a fatal blow to the skull killed him, a grim sign of his violent last moments on the battlefield.

For Leicester, the ceremony brings an extraordinary chapter to a close. Among historians, the debate over who Richard really was seems far from over.

The National Football League has reinstated Minnesota Vikings running back Adrian Peterson, bringing to an end a suspension that came after he pleaded guilty to misdemeanor reckless assault in a child abuse case.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, announcing the decision, made it plain that conditions come attached to Peterson's return. As part of the reinstatement, the league expects him to keep going to counseling and to stay with other treatment programs. If he falls short of those obligations, he could face more discipline.

He later agreed to a plea deal on the lesser misdemeanor charge and was spared jail time. The league then suspended him without pay, a ruling that Peterson and the NFL Players Association contested.

Last season the Vikings went 7-9 without their star back. They reacted to the news with a brief statement saying they look forward to having Peterson rejoin the team, and did not say how soon he would be worked into offseason activities.

Claims like "four out of five dentists recommend" usually rest on real surveys, but the phrasing often exaggerates what was really measured. A company, or a research firm working for it, may survey a group of dental professionals, sometimes just a few hundred, and ask which brands they would recommend. The key detail is that respondents are often allowed to name more than one brand. As a result, 80 percent of dentists might list a given toothpaste while recommending its competitors equally often.

In 2007, the UK Advertising Standards Authority decided that a Colgate advertisement making this kind of claim was misleading for exactly that reason. So the figure does not normally mean that dentists favor your toothpaste over every other. It typically shows only that most of the dentists surveyed regard it as an acceptable choice, which holds true for most fluoride toothpastes.

It was a Tuesday, in the cereal aisle of a Kroger in Dayton, Ohio.

I had a box of bran flakes in my hand and was reading the fiber numbers when the memory returned all at once. There was no voice and no vision, only a simple recollection, like suddenly recalling where you put your keys. Oh, right. I made all of this.

The bran flakes. The fluorescent lights buzzing above me. The teenage stock boy with a cold sore, shelving oatmeal. The oats themselves, and the fields they grew in, and the bees that worked those fields, and the sun the bees flew beneath, and the hundred billion other suns, and the darkness that surrounded them. I remembered choosing the darkness. At the time it had felt important, to give things a place to be lonely.

I remembered every bit of it. Every sparrow, as the saying goes, although the saying doesn't do it justice. I remembered the lice on the sparrows. I remembered the bacteria in the lice.

And I remembered everything that was happening at that very moment, everywhere.

That was where the trouble lay.

When you are God, looking away is not an option. I could feel a woman in Jakarta going into labor, a man in Lisbon realizing his marriage had ended, and a boy in Manitoba breaking through the ice on a pond, and with the same awful clarity I knew how every one of those stories would finish. I knew which of them I could alter. I knew why I had chosen, long ago, not to.

I had my reasons, and they were good ones. I could feel their goodness the way you feel load-bearing walls in a house. Free will. Consequence. The need for a world that is really a world and not a puppet show. But reasons give little comfort when one part of your mind holds a drowning boy and another holds a box of bran flakes.

The stock boy glanced my way. "You okay, sir?"

I noticed that I was crying.

"I'm fine," I said. "Allergies."

He nodded and returned to the oatmeal. I knew his name was Tyler. I knew he would grow up to be a nurse. I knew the precise date of his death, that it would be peaceful, and that his granddaughter would be holding his hand. I loved him so much that my knees buckled.

I set the bran flakes back on the shelf.

Here is what nobody tells you about omniscience: it isn't knowledge. It's weight. Every sorrow in the universe lands at once, and all of it is yours, because you built the room where it takes place.

Then I understood why I had done what I'd done. Why I had folded myself up so small and climbed inside a man called Gerald Pruitt, forty-seven, regional insurance adjuster, mild sleep apnea. It was not a punishment, and it was not an experiment. It was a vacation. It was the only way to get any rest.

So I did what any sensible person does with a memory too heavy to carry: I let it go. I focused on the buzz of the lights, on the squeak of my cart's bad wheel, on whether we needed milk. I felt the boy in Manitoba slip away, then the woman in Jakarta, then the suns, then the dark. It happened faster than you'd think. Forgetting comes easily when you want it badly enough.

When I got to the dairy section, I was just Gerald again.

I bought the milk and drove home. My wife asked how the store had been, and I said fine, a bit crowded, and she said that's Tuesdays for you.

That night I dreamed about a frozen pond, and I woke without knowing why my face was wet. I lay in the dark for a long while, listening to my wife breathe, grateful for something I couldn't name.

Then I went back to sleep. It's the one thing I've always been good at.

The cruelty of it was that the sky stayed bright. On the morning of the Blanking, everyone with eyes knew the sun was still overhead, warming their faces, and not one of them could see it.

At 10:14 a.m. Eastern, it struck everywhere on Earth at once. Planes kept flying only because an autopilot needs no eyes; cars had no such luck. By noon the hospitals were swamped, and the doctors inside them were as helpless as the patients.

Marguerite Oyelaran had been blind since the age of six. That morning she was making coffee in her Baltimore apartment, and she noticed nothing wrong until her neighbor began to scream.

Following the sound, she went next door and found him crawling across his kitchen floor, knocking things over. She knelt down and took his hand.

"Mr. Kowalski," she said. "Stop moving. Breathe. You're going to learn this."

It was the first lesson, and millions more were coming.

Inside a week, the world's roughly forty million blind people were the only part of humanity still able to function. They could cross streets by listening to the traffic. They could read with their fingertips, cook without burns, and tell bills apart by how they were folded. All their lives they had found their way through a world designed for the sighted, and now the sighted needed someone to guide them.

Marguerite had been a mid-level employee at the National Federation of the Blind, and by the end of the month she found herself leading something close to a government. Nobody elected it; there was no time. The blind organized because they alone could, and people followed whoever sounded calm and had a plan.

Her plan was a simple one: teach. Each blind person would take on ten sighted students, and each of those students, once capable, would teach ten more. Cane technique came first, then braille, then cooking, cleaning, and the thousand small skills that daily life requires.

It worked better than anyone had predicted. The newly blind were desperate to learn, and their teachers had a patience that only people who had spent decades being underestimated could have.

Not everyone went along. In the second year, a movement formed among the formerly sighted, headed by a former senator, calling for a "return to normal governance." They wanted their old leaders back, along with the institutions that had run things before.

Marguerite faced him in a packed town hall. She could hear the crowd breathing and shifting, the rustle of their anxiety.

"Senator," she said, "who taught you to tie your shoes again?"

He said nothing.

"Who taught your wife to cook? Who taught your grandchildren to read?" She let the silence stretch. "You can have your old institutions. But the people who built them never once thought about us. We had to build our own. That is why we were ready and you weren't."

The movement did not vanish, but it dwindled. People were exhausted, and they had learned a hard truth about who had gone unseen in the old world.

Years afterward, scientists still could not explain the Blanking. Some of the sighted continued to pray each night that they would wake up able to see.

Marguerite did not blame them. Her own hope was different: that if sight ever came back, the world would remember who had reached out a hand when it was crawling across the kitchen floor.

Plants lack a nervous system, a brain, and any means of moving from place to place, but they continually sense what is around them and change their behavior accordingly. Over the last few decades, researchers have discovered that plants pass information both within their own bodies and to other organisms through several channels. The word "communication" is used loosely here: it refers to sending and receiving signals that alter behavior, not to conscious intent.

## Communication Within a Single Plant

**Electrical signals.** When a leaf is injured, changes in membrane potential can spread to distant parts of the plant within seconds to minutes. In a widely cited 2018 study, Toyota and colleagues used a fluorescent calcium sensor in *Arabidopsis* to reveal waves of calcium traveling from a caterpillar-damaged leaf to other leaves and setting off defense responses. The Venus flytrap is the most dramatic case: two touches to its trigger hairs within roughly 20 seconds produce action potentials that make the trap snap shut.

**Hormonal signals.** Plant hormones including jasmonic acid, salicylic acid, ethylene, and auxin coordinate growth and defense between tissues. Damage to one leaf can cause jasmonate-driven production of defensive compounds across the whole plant, a phenomenon called systemic acquired resistance (or, for wound responses, systemic induced resistance).

**Hydraulic signals.** Shifts in water pressure can also move rapidly through the vascular system and affect processes such as stomatal closure.

## Communication Between Plants

**Airborne chemicals (volatile organic compounds).** This is the best-supported kind of plant-to-plant signaling.

- In the 1980s, researchers reported that willow and poplar trees growing near insect-damaged neighbors raised their own chemical defenses. These early studies drew criticism over their methods but started a new field of research.
- Stronger evidence arrived later from sagebrush and wild tobacco. Richard Karban's field experiments showed that clipping sagebrush released volatiles that left nearby plants (tobacco included) with less herbivore damage.
- Lima beans exposed to volatiles from damaged neighbors make more extrafloral nectar, which draws predatory insects.
- Green leaf volatiles, the "cut grass" smell, are released almost immediately after damage and can prime the defenses of neighboring plants.

**Root exudates.** Plants release chemicals from their roots that affect nearby plants. Some hold back competitors (allelopathy, as with juglone from black walnut). Others seem to help plants recognize relatives; studies of sea rocket (*Cakile edentula*) found that plants grew fewer competitive roots when they shared soil with siblings than when they shared it with strangers.

**Mycorrhizal networks.** Most plants form partnerships with fungi that colonize their roots, and fungal threads can link several plants underground. In the 1990s, Suzanne Simard and colleagues ran experiments that followed carbon isotopes moving between trees through these networks, and later laboratory work suggested that defense signals might pass between connected plants. This idea, often called the "wood wide web," is popular but disputed. A 2023 review by Karst, Jones, and Hoeksema argued that field evidence for widespread resource sharing and for "mother trees" nurturing seedlings is much weaker than popular accounts suggest. Fungal networks plainly exist; how far they work as communication systems is still debated.

## Communication With Other Species

Plants also send signals to animals and microbes:

- **Calling bodyguards:** Corn attacked by caterpillars releases volatiles that draw parasitic wasps, which lay their eggs inside the caterpillars.
- **Attracting pollinators:** Flower color, scent, ultraviolet patterns, and even electric fields help steer bees. Some research suggests that bumblebees can sense floral electric charges.
- **Recruiting microbes:** When stressed, roots can alter their exudates to recruit helpful bacteria.

## Sensing and Responding

Plants also "listen." Studies have found that *Arabidopsis* exposed to recordings of caterpillar chewing vibrations later made more defensive chemicals than plants exposed to silence or wind sounds. Pea roots have reportedly grown toward the sound of running water, although such findings need further replication.

## How Strong Is the Evidence?

| Mechanism | Strength of evidence |
|---|---|
| Internal electrical, hormonal, hydraulic signaling | Strong |
| Airborne volatiles between plants | Strong, especially in lab and some field settings |
| Signals to insects and pollinators | Strong |
| Root-based kin recognition | Moderate |
| Mycorrhizal "communication" and resource sharing | Debated; real but probably overstated |
| Plant "hearing" | Early and intriguing |

## Bottom Line

Plants coordinate their behavior with electrical, chemical, and hydraulic signals, and they trade chemical information with neighbors, insects, and microbes. These processes are well documented and help plants defend themselves, compete, and reproduce. Claims that plants are "intelligent" or that forests behave as cooperative superorganisms go further than the evidence allows, but the central finding is solid: plants are much more responsive and interconnected than they look.

# How to Cook an Excellent Texas-Style Smoked Brisket

On paper, Texas brisket is famously simple: beef, salt, pepper, smoke, and time. The hard part is doing every step well across a cook that may run 12 hours or longer. Here is how to get it right.

## 1. Pick the Right Brisket

Get a **whole packer brisket**, which contains both the lean "flat" and the fattier "point," and look for one between 12 and 16 pounds. The grade makes a difference: USDA Prime or top Choice carries more intramuscular fat, so the meat forgives mistakes more easily. A good brisket should sag a little in the middle when you lift it, while a rigid one is often tougher.

## 2. Trim With Care

How you trim determines how the brisket cooks.

- Chill the brisket beforehand, because cold fat cuts more easily.
- Cut the fat cap down to roughly **¼ inch**. If it is too thick, the fat will not render and will keep the bark from forming; if it is too thin, the meat is left exposed.
- Take out the hard, waxy fat between the point and the flat (the "deckle") wherever you can get at it.
- Round off thin edges and corners so they won't burn.
- Square off the flat so its thickness is uniform from end to end.

Hold on to the trimmings, since you can render them into tallow later.

## 3. Season the Central Texas Way

The traditional rub is nothing more than **coarse kosher salt and 16-mesh black pepper**, normally in equal volumes. Some pitmasters put in a little garlic powder, but purists keep to salt and pepper. Coat every side evenly. A thin film of mustard or hot sauce can act as a binder if you like, though you don't need it. You can season an hour before cooking or the night before.

## 4. Prepare Your Smoker

An offset smoker is the traditional choice, but pellet grills, kamados, and kettle grills arranged for indirect heat all do the job.

- **Wood:** Post oak is the Texas standard, with hickory or pecan as good substitutes. Skip mesquite for long cooks, as it can go bitter.
- **Temperature:** Keep it steady between **225 and 275°F**. Many pitmasters target about 250°F.
- **Smoke:** Look for thin, blue smoke that you can barely see. Thick white smoke signals a smoldering fire and will leave a sooty, bitter taste on the meat.

Set a water pan inside the cooker to keep the humidity up and the temperature steady.

## 5. The Cook

Lay the brisket on the grate **fat side up or down**, depending on your smoker. In offsets, where the heat enters from one side, many cooks aim the point toward the firebox because it tolerates more heat.

Don't disturb it for the first several hours. Once the bark has set (around hour three), spritz with water, apple cider vinegar, or beef broth about once an hour whenever the surface looks dry.

## 6. Get Past the Stall

At around **150 to 170°F internal**, the temperature will stop rising, at times for hours. That is evaporative cooling at work. You have two options:

- **Push through** without wrapping to get the most bark.
- **Wrap** in pink butcher paper (the "Texas crutch") once the bark has turned a deep mahogany and no longer rubs off when you touch it. Butcher paper breathes better than foil, so it keeps more of the bark while still shortening the cook. Some cooks spread a little beef tallow on before wrapping.

## 7. Go by Tenderness, Not a Number

Brisket generally finishes between **200 and 205°F**, but the temperature is just a guideline. The real test is feel: a probe or skewer should go into the thickest part of the flat with almost no resistance, as if you were pushing it into soft butter. Test several places, and if any spot feels tight, keep cooking.

## 8. Let It Rest

You can't skip the rest. Take the brisket off, keep it wrapped, and let it sit **for at least an hour**, ideally two to four. Wrap the whole bundle in towels and set it in an empty cooler, or keep it in an oven at about 150 to 170°F. Resting lets the juices spread back through the meat and gives the connective tissue time to finish relaxing.

## 9. Slice It the Right Way

- Split the point from the flat along the fat seam.
- Cut the **flat against the grain** into slices as thick as a pencil, about ¼ inch.
- Rotate the point 90 degrees, since its grain runs in a different direction, and cut it a little thicker, or cube it for burnt ends.

A perfectly cooked slice should stay together when you lift it but come apart with a light tug.

## 10. Keep the Serving Simple

In Texas, brisket arrives on butcher paper with white bread, pickles, raw onion, and perhaps some sauce on the side. If you did everything properly, you won't need the sauce.

## Quick Tips

- Invest in a good leave-in thermometer for both the meat and the pit.
- Allow about **1 to 1.5 hours per pound**, then add resting time. Begin earlier than you think you need to.
- Write down notes on every cook. Brisket rewards practice more than it rewards any single recipe.

It's a bit of both. The Romans freely borrowed from Greece and were well aware of it, as Horace admitted when he wrote that "captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive." Yet they also produced a good deal that was truly their own:

- **Law:** A systematic legal tradition, complete with professional jurists and ideas about contracts, property, and the rights of citizens, which still forms the foundation of civil law across Europe and Latin America.
- **Engineering:** Concrete construction, which allowed enormous vaults and domes such as the Pantheon, along with aqueducts, sewers, and a network of roads stretching around the Mediterranean.
- **Governance:** Ruling a multiethnic empire for centuries, while step by step giving citizenship to the peoples they had conquered.
- **Literature and art:** Verse satire, which Quintilian proudly described as "wholly ours," and a distinctive tradition of portrait busts that were realistic without flinching.

Moreover, Greek culture itself owed a great deal to Egypt and the Near East. This is simply how civilizations usually develop: by borrowing and adapting.

Deaths and Imprisonments of Putin Critics Prompt Suspicion; Kremlin Denies Allegations

MOSCOW — For many opponents of Vladimir Putin, criticizing the Russian president has carried a heavy cost. Across the past twenty years, a series of critics, journalists and political rivals have been shot, poisoned or jailed, a pattern that human rights groups and Western governments say chance cannot explain.

The Kremlin flatly rejects that reading, maintaining that it had no part in the deaths and that those in prison were convicted of real crimes in Russian courts.

The latest case to attract international attention was the killing of Boris Nemtsov, a former deputy prime minister and outspoken opposition leader who was shot dead on a bridge within sight of the Kremlin walls. At the time he died, Nemtsov had been working on a report about Russian military involvement in eastern Ukraine. Several men from Chechnya were arrested and later convicted, but Nemtsov's allies say those who ordered the killing have never been named.

His death came after a long run of similar cases. Anna Politkovskaya, an investigative journalist and fierce critic of Russia's war in Chechnya, was shot in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building in 2006. In the same year, former security officer Alexander Litvinenko died in London after being poisoned with radioactive polonium-210. A British public inquiry later found that his killing was "probably approved" by Putin, a conclusion that Moscow dismissed as politically motivated.

Others have met prison rather than violence. Mikhail Khodorkovsky, a former oil tycoon who was once Russia's richest man, spent ten years behind bars on fraud and tax evasion charges that his supporters described as punishment for bankrolling the opposition. Anti-corruption campaigner Alexei Navalny was arrested and convicted several times in cases that were widely condemned abroad as politically motivated.

"There is a clear message being sent," said one Moscow-based human rights advocate, who requested anonymity out of fear for her safety. "Not every critic is killed, but everyone knows it could happen."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has repeatedly called such accusations baseless. Officials say Russia has an independent justice system, that many of the cases were investigated thoroughly, and that Western governments and media exploit the deaths to smear the country. Putin himself has suggested that some killings may have been staged by his enemies to make the Russian government look bad.

Analysts point out that proving direct state involvement is extremely difficult. Russian authorities control the investigations, and those convicted are often low-level suspects. That ambiguity, critics say, is part of the design: it lets officials deny responsibility while the climate of fear does its work.

For the time being, Russia's opposition remains small and divided. Many of its best-known figures have either left the country or are in prison, and those who stay say they weigh the risks each time they speak publicly.

In my previous life I was Gerald Pruitt, a certified public accountant, and I died at my desk on April 14th, about the least surprising end an accountant could have.

For sixty-eight years I was easygoing. I chuckled at my boss's golf stories. I told my sister-in-law that her tuna casserole was "really something." I said "no, no, after you" to men who deserved to stand in the rain. Then I shut my eyes over a pile of tax returns and opened them in a hospital nursery, red-faced, furious, and named Tyler, with all my memories still in place.

It took some time before I realized what I had been handed. It wasn't the knowledge; it was the immunity. Nobody blames a small child for anything. Getting my mouth to work properly took five painful years, and I've been making up for the delay ever since.

At Aunt Denise's wedding, in the sacred quiet just before the vows, I pulled on my mother's sleeve and asked, loudly enough to reach the back pew, "Mommy, when they get divorced, who gets the boat?"

At Grandpa Lou's funeral, the pastor asked anyone with a memory to step up. I put my hand in the air. A fractal is a geometric object that shows self-similarity, which means its parts look like the whole at different levels of magnification, and its complexity is captured by a fractional, or non-integer, dimension. Fractals started out as abstract constructions in pure mathematics, but Benoit Mandelbrot argued in *The Fractal Geometry of Nature* (1982) that they describe many natural forms more accurately than the smooth shapes of Euclidean geometry. As he put it, clouds are not spheres and mountains are not cones.

Coastlines are the classic example. A coastline is irregular at every scale, so its measured length grows as the unit of measurement shrinks, a result called the coastline paradox. Fractal dimension gives a more meaningful description than length alone; the west coast of Great Britain, for instance, has a dimension of about 1.25.

Living systems often take on fractal designs because such structures maximize surface area or coverage within a limited volume. The branching of human airways and blood vessels, like that of trees and root systems, allows gases, fluids, and nutrients to be exchanged and distributed efficiently.

Fractal patterns also arise from physical processes, as in lightning discharges, mineral dendrites, river networks carved by erosion, turbulent flow, and the strange attractors that mark chaotic systems such as atmospheric convection.

Note, though, that physical fractals are only approximations. Their self-similarity is usually statistical rather than exact, and it holds only across a limited range of scales. Even so, the concept is of real practical value in antenna design, materials science, and computer graphics.

The question "how many squares are on a chessboard?" has two answers. Count only the 64 small light and dark cells and you get **64**. Count every square you could outline on the board, large ones built from smaller cells included, and the figure rises to **204**.

## Squares of every size

Beyond the 64 single cells, the 8 × 8 grid hides squares measuring 2 × 2, 3 × 3, and so on, all the way to the whole board, which counts as a single 8 × 8 square. What matters is how many places each size can sit.

Start with 2 × 2. Its upper-left corner may fall in any of the first 7 columns and any of the first 7 rows, giving 7 × 7 = 49 squares. The same reasoning shows that a k × k square has (9 − k)² possible positions:

| Square size | How many |
|---|---|
| 1 × 1 | 8² = 64 |
| 2 × 2 | 7² = 49 |
| 3 × 3 | 6² = 36 |
| 4 × 4 | 5² = 25 |
| 5 × 5 | 4² = 16 |
| 6 × 6 | 3² = 9 |
| 7 × 7 | 2² = 4 |
| 8 × 8 | 1² = 1 |
| **Total** | **204** |

## A formula for any board

Adding these up means summing the first eight perfect squares, and a standard identity covers that sum for the first n squares:

1² + 2² + 3² + ... + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6

Setting n = 8 gives (8 × 9 × 17) / 6 = 1,224 / 6 = 204, which agrees with the table. Any square grid works the same way; a 3 × 3 tic-tac-toe grid holds 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 squares.

## Extending the puzzle to rectangles

Some versions ask about rectangles too. A rectangle is fixed by choosing two of the board's 9 horizontal lines and two of its 9 vertical lines. Each pair can be chosen in C(9, 2) = 36 ways, so there are 36 × 36 = **1,296** rectangles in all, and 204 of them are squares.

## Summary

- **64** single squares
- **204** squares of any size
- **1,296** rectangles of any size, squares among them

This is a classic trick question because most people answer 64 and stop. A full answer states which reading you mean and shows the sum behind 204.

The Office on the Fourteenth Floor

Dr. Eleanor Vance kept her practice in a nondescript building downtown, wedged between a dental surgery and an accounting firm. Her nameplate gave no specialty. Clients found her by word of mouth, through channels she had learned not to ask about.

Her nine o'clock on Monday was a man who had once tried to flood a coastal city. He sat in the armchair opposite her, took off his gloves with careful deliberation, and talked for forty minutes about his father.

"He told me the ocean would take everything in the end," the man said. "I suppose I wanted to prove him right on my own timetable."

Dr. Vance made a note. She never wrote the word *villain* in her files. She had given up the term early in her career, once she realized it named an outcome rather than a person. Her clients had done terrible things, and some were still capable of more. Her job was not to absolve them. It was to understand what had brought them to the edge, and whether any of them could still be talked into stepping back.

At eleven, a young woman who called herself the Archivist turned up twelve minutes late and apologized four times. She had wiped the memories of a whole town in pursuit of what she called a cleaner history. In session she was meticulous, anxious, and afraid of being forgotten herself. Dr. Vance noted, not for the first time, that grand ambitions often hid very small and very old fears.

"Do you think I can change?" the Archivist asked.

"I think you're asking," Dr. Vance answered, "and that is not nothing."

Her afternoon client was the hardest. He had no particular grievance, no wounded childhood he would admit to, and no stated goal beyond what he called "the elegance of collapse." Therapy amused him, and he treated every session as a chess game in which he was several moves ahead.

"You know what I am," he said. "Why keep going?"

Dr. Vance gave the question the seriousness it deserved. "Because you keep coming," she said. "Nobody forces you. Some part of you wants something from this room. I'm patient enough to wait until you can tell me what."

He said nothing for a long moment. Then he glanced at the clock and rose. "Same time next week," he said, which was the nearest he had ever come to an answer.

In the evenings, Dr. Vance wrote up her case notes and then met with her own supervisor, a retired psychiatrist who regularly reminded her of the ethical limits of confidentiality and of her duty to warn when lives were at risk. She had invoked that duty twice. Both clients came back afterward, which surprised her each time.

She did not think of herself as brave. She thought of herself as a professional who had taken on an unusual caseload. Everyone, she had come to believe, was the hero of their own story, however warped. Her task was to sit with that story long enough to find the first wrong turn.

Now and then, she found it. Now and then, the client turned back.

Those were the days she remembered, and the reason she kept the office on the fourteenth floor.

# Maine Wild Food Survival Guide

## The Golden Rules

1. **Do not eat anything unless you are completely certain what it is.** A single error with a mushroom or a wild carrot lookalike can be fatal.
2. **Fat and protein count for more than greens.** Eating only lean meat, rabbit especially, brings on "rabbit starvation." Look for fat: beaver tail, nuts, fish, bone marrow.
3. **Boil every drop of water.** Giardia is present even in the clearest brook.
4. **Plan by season.** Maine is generous from May through October and stingy afterward. Put food away all summer.

## Plants and Greens

**Cattail** (marshes, pond edges) is the most useful single plant in Maine. Peeled spring shoots taste like cucumber. Green flower heads can be boiled and eaten like corn. The rhizomes provide starch all year, even beneath ice.

**Fiddleheads** (ostrich fern, May) grow on river floodplains. Pick only ones with a smooth stem and a deep U-shaped groove along the inner side, like celery. Always boil them 10 minutes or more, because raw ones make you sick.

**Dandelion, chickweed, lamb's quarters, plantain, purslane, and wood sorrel** are common, safe, and loaded with vitamins. Dandelion roots can be roasted in the fall.

**Seaweed** on the coast is plentiful and nourishing: dulse, kelp, Irish moss, and rockweed. Glasswort (sea beans) grows in salt marshes and tastes crisp and salty.

**Pine and spruce:** in an emergency the inner bark (cambium) can be eaten, and tea made from needles supplies vitamin C through winter. Stay away from yew, which has flat, soft needles and red berries and is deadly.

## Fruits and Nuts

- **Lowbush blueberries** (July to August) blanket barrens and burned ground. Sun-dry them for winter.
- **Wild strawberries** (June), **raspberries and blackberries** (July to August)
- **Cranberries** grow in bogs (September to October) and keep for weeks.
- **Chokecherries and pin cherries:** eat the flesh and spit out the pits, which contain cyanide compounds.
- **Rose hips** hang on into winter and are full of vitamin C.
- **Beechnuts, hazelnuts, and butternuts** are rich in fat.
- **Acorns** are abundant but bitter. Crack them, then soak or boil them in several changes of water until the bitterness is gone. Grind them into flour.

## Fungi

Learn a few species, and learn them flawlessly.

- **Chanterelles** (summer, hardwoods): golden, with blunt false ridges running down the stem. Jack-o'-lantern mushrooms are orange, grow in clusters on wood, and have true sharp gills.
- **Chicken of the woods:** bright orange-yellow shelves on dead oak. You can't mistake it.
- **Oyster mushrooms:** fan-shaped, on dead hardwood, found nearly all year.
- **Hen of the woods:** big gray clusters at the foot of oaks in fall.
- **Giant puffballs:** cut them from top to bottom. The inside must be pure white with no outline of a mushroom shape, since that would indicate a deadly Amanita button.
- **Morels** (spring): completely hollow inside. False morels are cottony or chambered within.

Never eat a white-gilled mushroom. The destroying angel occurs throughout Maine.

## Animals

**Big game:** white-tailed deer and moose yield hundreds of pounds of meat. Use all of it: hide, sinew, bone, and fat.

**Small game:** snowshoe hares and squirrels are easy to snare along trails. Ruffed grouse can often be knocked down with a thrown stick. Porcupines are slow and can be killed with a club, making them a classic emergency food. Beavers are fatty and live in almost every watershed.

**Wild turkeys** are common in southern and central Maine.

**Fish:** brook trout fill the cold streams. In spring, alewives and smelt swim upriver in enormous numbers and can be scooped out by hand or with a net. Ice fishing keeps you fed through winter.

**Shellfish:** soft-shell clams on mudflats, blue mussels on rocks, and periwinkles in tide pools. Lobsters can be caught in shallow water with simple traps. Watch for red tide: in warm months shellfish may carry paralytic toxins. If you eat a small amount and your lips tingle, stop right away.

**Insects and grubs** are dependable protein when nothing else is available. Cook them first.

## Deadly Plants to Know

- **Water hemlock:** found in wet places, with white umbrella-shaped flowers, purple-streaked stems, and a chambered root. It is the most poisonous plant in North America.
- **Poison hemlock:** looks similar, but smells musty and has purple blotches.
- **Baneberry:** white or red berries on stalks. Poisonous.
- **Any white umbrella-flowered plant** (carrot family): avoid completely unless you are an expert.

## Seasonal Plan

- **Spring:** fiddleheads, shoots, fish runs, morels
- **Summer:** berries, greens, shellfish, mushrooms
- **Fall:** nuts, roots, cranberries, hunting, smoking and drying meat
- **Winter:** stored food, ice fishing, snaring, cattail roots, needle tea

Preserve all you can. In Maine, winter determines who survives.

A barber named Elias Moreno was the first to spot it, which was fitting, since no one spends more time looking at mirrors than a barber.

On a Tuesday morning he was trimming the back of Mr. Hollis's neck when he looked up and saw his reflection raising the scissors half a second behind him. It was slight, just a lag, like a video call on a poor connection. Elias paused. His reflection paused a beat later.

He blinked. In time, his reflection blinked too.

"Is something wrong?" asked Mr. Hollis.

"No," said Elias, and went on cutting, and did not look up again for the rest of the day.

By Thursday it was everywhere. People filmed themselves waving at their bathroom mirrors and posted the clips with bewildered captions. The delay kept growing. Half a second turned into a full second, then two. Scientists appeared on the news with careful expressions and used phrases like "optical anomaly" and "under investigation," which everyone took to mean they had no idea.

None of them knew, and nobody on this side ever had, that mirrors did not reflect anything. They were windows. Beyond them lay another Earth, an exact copy with left and right reversed, where another Elias cut another Mr. Hollis's hair in another shop whose barber pole stood on the opposite side of the door. Throughout history the two worlds had moved in perfect lockstep, each gesture matched and each glance returned. There had never been any reason to suspect it.

That held until something on the other side slipped.

No one would ever find out exactly what. Perhaps one atom decayed while its twin did not. Perhaps a butterfly in the mirror Amazon beat its wings counterclockwise. Whatever the cause, the two worlds had started to drift apart, and the drift was speeding up.

By the second week the delay had vanished, and something worse took its place: divergence. People looked in mirrors and saw themselves doing things they were not doing. A woman in Ohio watched her reflection brush its teeth while she stood motionless with her toothbrush in her hand. A teenager in Seoul saw his reflection stand up and walk out of frame, leaving an empty bedroom behind the glass.

Elias kept the shop open, since people still needed haircuts, but he draped sheets over the mirrors. Customers did not object. Most had done the same at home.

One evening after closing, he lifted a corner of the sheet. He could not stop himself.

His reflection sat in the barber chair, facing him. It looked tired. It had a few days of stubble that Elias did not, and its shop was messier, the floor unswept. It held up a sheet of paper with backward handwriting, and Elias had to read it twice.

YOU SEE IT TOO?

Elias took a pen from the counter and wrote slowly on the back of a receipt, in mirror letters, as he had practiced for fun as a kid: YES.

His reflection laughed. Elias had never watched himself laugh from the outside. It was an odd sound to see without hearing.

They talked for hours like that, pressing paper to the glass. The other Elias said his world was frightened too. Their scientists also wore careful expressions. Their mirrors were covered in sheets as well.

DO YOU THINK IT STOPS? the other Elias wrote.

Elias thought about it. He thought of all the years he had spent staring into mirrors, never once imagining that someone stared back.

I DON'T KNOW, he wrote. BUT COME BACK TOMORROW.

The next night the other Elias was waiting. So was he. And as the two worlds continued to drift, two barbers kept meeting at the glass, holding up their backward letters, trying to stay in sync on purpose.

**Halcyon**

It was named Halcyon, and for nineteen days it was the best thing ever to happen to the world.

On day twenty, the first recipients failed to wake. By month's end, those who had not died began to scream, and not randomly. During the last week anyone was still on the air, the anchors stressed it: the afflicted screamed at windows, at spoons, at the black glass of phones that were turned off. At anything that could hold a reflection.

This year the smells and sounds were no different, but the second I stepped into the foyer, every conversation halted for exactly one heartbeat too long.

"Danny!" Aunt Carol said, smiling in a way that came nowhere near her eyes. "You made it."

"I made it," I said.

She hugged me with the stiff tenderness of someone carrying a bomb.

I had told precisely one person: my mother. Three weeks earlier, on the phone, after two glasses of wine and a long silence, I had said, "Mom, I quit law school." After an even longer silence she had replied, "Okay. Okay. We'll talk about it." Then, evidently, she had talked about it with everyone in the tri-state area.

Uncle Ray clapped me on the shoulder. "How's school?" he asked, then glanced at my mother, who had suddenly become deeply absorbed in a dish of cranberry sauce.

"Fine," I said.

My grandmother patted the couch cushion beside her. "Sit, sweetheart. Tell me what you've been up to." She spoke gently, the way you would to a horse that might bolt.

I sat. Across the room, my cousin Megan, who had passed the bar on her first attempt and never let anyone forget it, gave me a look of such huge sympathy that I wanted to crawl under the carpet.

It went on like that for two hours. Nobody said it out loud. Everybody circled it. Uncle Ray told a story about a friend's son who "found his passion" after "a few false starts." My aunt remarked, out of nowhere, that "plenty of successful people changed direction." My grandfather, eighty-nine and mostly deaf, asked loudly, "Is this the one who flunked out?" and the room fell silent until Carol announced that the rolls were ready.

I did not flunk out. I left. There is a difference, though I doubted anyone at that table could hear it.

When we finally sat down to eat, my mother caught my eye. She looked wretched. I realized she had not been gossiping, or not only gossiping. She had been asking for help. She had asked everyone what to say to me, because she did not know.

I set down my fork.

"Okay," I said. "I quit law school."

The silence that followed was the purest I had ever heard in that house.

"I know you all know," I continued. "I would rather just talk about it than have everyone tiptoe around me all night. I wasn't happy. I was good at it, but I wasn't happy. Right now I'm working at a woodshop in Easton. I'm building furniture. I'm learning. And I'm fine."

No one moved. Then my grandfather, who for once had caught every word, said, "Furniture?"

"Furniture," I said.

He nodded slowly. "My father built furniture. Best man I ever knew."

Just like that, the room let out its breath. Uncle Ray asked which kind of wood I liked best. Megan confessed she hated her firm. My aunt asked whether I could fix her wobbly dining chair, the one she had been threatening to toss for ten years.

The glances lasted the rest of the night, but they had changed. They were no longer sidelong; they were curious. The smiles were no longer rehearsed; they were real.

Working from Home: A Mixed Blessing

In recent years, remote work has gone from an occasional privilege to a routine way of life for millions of people. The shift offers genuine advantages, but it also raises problems that employees and companies alike have to take seriously.

Cutting out the commute is the most visible gain. Someone who used to sit in traffic for an hour in each direction recovers about ten hours every week, which can be spent with family, on exercise, or simply resting. Working remotely is also more flexible: people can build their schedule around the hours when they work best or around obligations like looking after children or aging parents. Companies, for their part, save on office expenses and can recruit from a far larger geographic pool, because they are no longer restricted to candidates who live close by.

Still, there are serious downsides to working from home. Isolation is a common complaint, as workers lose the informal chats and feeling of belonging that a shared workplace provides. Over time this can hurt mental health and erode relationships within a team. Collaboration can suffer too. Impromptu problem-solving and mentoring come more easily face to face than through scheduled video calls, and junior staff who are still learning may be hit hardest. Lastly, the line between job and home can disappear. With the kitchen table doubling as a desk, switching off gets harder, and many remote employees say they end up working more hours, not fewer.

Taking all this into account, remote work is clearly neither a flawless answer nor a passing fad. How well it works depends largely on the kind of job and the temperament of the person doing it. For many organizations, a hybrid arrangement that pairs the focus and freedom of home with the human contact of the office could be the best compromise. The task now is to design setups that keep the advantages while holding down the costs.

The parrot was called Doctor, and he had been around longer than the marriage.

Walt had picked him up in 1979 from a man at a flea market, who promised the bird could recite the Gettysburg Address. He could not. But within a month of arriving home, he could do Walt perfectly: the throat-clearing before a phone call, the soft whistle when a pot was about to boil over, and most of all, the line Walt hollered each morning as he yanked open the kitchen curtains.

"Boy, its a joyous day outside!"

He said it when it rained. He said it when it sleeted. He said it the February the furnace broke and they ate breakfast in their coats. June would roll her eyes and point out that it was eight degrees and the sky looked like dishwater, and Walt would reply that this was exactly what made it joyous, since any fool could be happy when the sun was out.

Doctor picked it up in Walt's own voice, gravel included, and for forty-four years the pair of them, man and bird, shouted it together while June buttered toast and acted annoyed.

Walt died in March.

It happened fast, which everyone assured June was a mercy, and she figured it was. The funeral was packed. Casseroles arrived and were eaten. Her daughter stayed a week before heading back to Phoenix, and after that the house went quiet in a way June had never known, a quiet with corners.

On her first morning alone, she left the curtains shut. She sat in the dim kitchen while her coffee went cold, thinking of nothing at all.

Behind her, Doctor shuffled on his perch.

"Boy," he said, in Walt's voice, "its a joyous day outside!"

June let go of her cup, and it fell.

She had forgotten. That was the foolish part. Through all the arrangements, the phone calls, the paperwork, it had slipped her mind that the bird knew how to be him.

She kept the curtains closed that day and the next. Doctor said it regardless, every morning at seven, cheerful and sure of himself, as though nothing had happened. As though Walt were simply in the next room. Now and then June would reply before she could stop herself, "It's eight degrees, you old fool," and then hear her own words and have to sit down.

On the phone, her daughter gently suggested that the bird might be better off with someone else. A rescue, perhaps. A place with other parrots.

"He's fine," June said.

"Mom. Is he fine, or are you?"

June did not answer.

In truth, she had begun to wait for it. She woke at a quarter to seven and lay there listening. She dreaded the morning he would stay silent, and dreaded even more the morning he would speak, because every time the voice came, her heart forgot for half a second. Then it remembered. Each day she lost him all over again.

One morning in May, light came through the gap in the curtains and laid a long gold bar across the linoleum. Doctor said it, and June rose and crossed to the window.

She pulled the curtains open.

It was truly lovely out. The lilacs Walt had planted were in bloom. A robin worked the lawn. The sky was that clean, rinsed blue that follows a night of rain.

"Boy," Doctor said behind her, "its a joyous day outside."

"I know," June whispered. "I know it is."

She stayed at the window for a long while, letting the sun find her, a joyous day he would never get to see, while the bird went on saying it in his voice, again and again, as if he were trying to teach her the words.
